title: "Stock Markets and Private Capital"
affiliations: Professor of Commercial and Corporate Law (CUNEF)

detail.title: "Stock Markets and Private Capital"
detail.abstract: This paper deals with the economic decline that the stock markets are experiencing, in Spain and internationally, as a consequence of the progressive and apparently unstoppable reduction in the number of listed companies and their capital raising operations. This circumstance has given rise to a response from legislators and regulators in the European Union and on the Spanish market, although in this case the approach has been partial, contradictory and inconsistent. While most of the proposed reforms affect regulatory issues, the loss of attractiveness of the stock markets for many companies seems to be explained not only by certain changes in the nature of the companies in the new economy, but also and fundamentally by the colossal development that the private capital and credit markets have undergone in recent years. Private capital, by guaranteeing ample financing possibilities for companies and liquidity for their shareholders and founders, has largely replaced the functions traditionally performed by the stock markets. Private capital also allows for a structure of ownership, control and incentives within companies, giving rise, in general terms, to important economic and organizational advantages, in comparison with the stock markets. But there are still relevant legal policy arguments to try to revitalize the stock markets, such as the informative function they perform or the fact that they represent an essential channel for investment and participation by small investors in economic growth.

title: Return Trade-Offs between Biodiversity Physical and Transition Risk in Global Equity Markets
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest, Corvinus University of Budapest - Department of Finance and Corvinus University of Budapest

detail.title: Return Trade-Offs between Biodiversity Physical and Transition Risk in Global Equity Markets
detail.abstract: We investigate whether biodiversity-related risks are priced in global equity markets by testing whether firms' ecological pressures and dependencies are rewarded or penalized in return. We use firm-and portfolio-level data for over 2,000 global firms from 2019 to 2024, combining ENCORE ecosystem service pressure and dependency scores and Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators. Our findings show robust evidence of a biodiversity risk premium (BRP), demonstrating that both biodiversity physical (dependency-related) and biodiversity transition (pressure-related) risks are significantly priced in by equity markets. Moreover, consistent with prior literature, climate-related factors exhibit even stronger pricing effects; our results, however, reveal the distinct emergence of the BRP beyond previously documented findings. Results show that portfolios formed using ENCORE scores generate no significant abnormal returns, whereas PAI-based portfolios yield a consistent negative alpha for high-pressure firms. This underperformance is more pronounced in Europe and in the post-2022 period, coinciding with the development of EU sustainable finance regulations. Results suggest that disclosure frameworks, such as the EU's PAI, increase transparency and actively shape capital allocation and risk pricing.

title: Redesignig Internal Control Architecture in the Digital Era -Tech Adoption, Friction Points and Remedial Design Choices
affiliations: Central Bank of Bahrain

detail.title: Redesignig Internal Control Architecture in the Digital Era -Tech Adoption, Friction Points and Remedial Design Choices
detail.abstract:
Digital banks operate as continuously evolving technology platforms, yet they remain subject to control architectures designed for static, monolithic financial institutions with infrequent change cycles. This article examines the fundamental friction between traditional banking control frameworks-structured around periodic assurance, sequential approval gates, and the Three Lines of Defence-and the operational reality of digital banks characterized by continuous deployment, distributed ownership, and platform-based architectures. The paper argues that digital banks often fail not from absence of controls, but from control misdesign: overlay mechanisms that create compliance overlays that leads to delayed recognition of real-time risks embedded in code, APIs, and cloud infrastructure. 
Drawing on regulatory practice and platform engineering principles, it is clear that Digital Banks need a shift toward controls-by-design-embedding risk, compliance, and audit functions natively into CI/CD pipelines, policy-as-code frameworks, and site reliability engineering (SRE) disciplines. 
For supervisors, this requires moving beyond checklist reviews toward evaluating control effectiveness in motion, assessing architectural resilience, and understanding technology risk as existential business risk. The article concludes that traditional control architectures are not obsolete but must be fundamentally reengineered to remain credible and effective in digital banking environments.

title: Brave New China: Dystopia or Utopia?

detail.title: Brave New China: Dystopia or Utopia?
detail.abstract: If Aldous Huxley, the author of the first classic dystopian novel Brave New World, were to classify modern China as a dystopia or a utopia, he would in all likelihood describe China as a dystopia. After all, Huxley was an ardent believer in liberal democracy, and his main gripe with the Western political system (especially in the United States) was that it had failed to live up to its ideals. As such, Huxley would not be able to ignore the restrictions in China on direct participation in high-level decision-making. Huxley would likely have viewed China in much the same way as he viewed the Soviet Union of the 1950s: as a formidable rival and an uncomfortable reminder of the pitfalls of the Western system, but not a country to be emulated or necessarily admired. At the same time, even if Huxley would likely view China as a dystopia, his conception of a dystopia is very different from that of George Orwell. What Huxley feared most was not a violent and brutal dictatorship a la 1984 but rather a state that had mastered non-coercive manipulation and conditioning while providing its people with universal satisfaction. As this article argues, Huxley would probably have a level of respect for "Brave New China" and its ability to strike a “grand bargain” with its people to achieve genuine stability and a baseline of public satisfaction.

detail.abstract:
The European banking industry is undergoing fundamental transformation driven by open banking regulation, FinTech disruption, and shifting consumer expectations. The implementation of the revised Payment Services Directive (PSD2) in January 2018 effectively dismantled banks' traditional monopoly over customer financial data, enabling licensed third-party providers—particularly FinTech firms operating as Account Information Service Providers (AISPs) and Payment Initiation Service Providers (PISPs)—to access banking infrastructure and compete directly with incumbent institutions.

This paper addresses three interrelated research questions: (1) What is the impact of open banking on banks, and what role do FinTechs play in this transformation? (2) How does FinTech affect bank profitability and digitalisation strategies? (3) How are banks responding strategically to FinTech disruption? The study employs a mixed-methods research design combining systematic literature review with quantitative analysis of the World Bank's Global Findex Database 2025. Evidence is triangulated across academic literature, regulatory reports from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), the European Central Bank (ECB), and the Financial Stability Board (FSB), alongside industry surveys from McKinsey, Oliver Wyman, EY-Parthenon, and Finastra covering 28 European countries from 2018 to 2025. The Global Findex data shows that by 2024, 94.6% of Europeans owned an account and 91.8% used the internet, but there are still big differences between regions. Nordic countries consistently lead with internet penetration exceeding 98%, while Romania (76.9%) and Bulgaria (79.4%) exhibit lower digital infrastructure maturity, suggesting that Open Banking's impact varies substantially by market context.

Banks' strategic responses have evolved from viewing FinTechs as existential threats toward embracing 'coopetition' through partnership arrangements. Industry surveys indicate that 75% of banks plan to engage with multiple FinTechs, and only 6% pursue in-house development strategies. However, approximately 40% of bank-FinTech partnerships fail to operationalise due to legacy system integration challenges, priority misalignment, information asymmetry, and cultural disconnects between traditional banking culture and FinTech agility.

The paper concludes that open banking represents not an existential threat but an ecosystem restructuring that rewards strategic adaptation. Successful navigation requires banks to develop partnership capabilities that are characterised by deep strategic alignment, cultural compatibility, and sustained organisational commitment.

title: Energy-Anchored Fiscal Seigniorage: A Stock–Flow Consistent Dynamic Mode

detail.title: Energy-Anchored Fiscal Seigniorage: A Stock–Flow Consistent Dynamic Mode
detail.abstract: This paper develops a stock-flow consistent (SFC) dynamic model in which a rule-based component of base-money creation is tied to real energy production and transferred to the Treasury as spendable seigniorage. The model rigorously distinguishes stocks from flows, separates base money from deposit creation, embeds a Keynesian goods-market block, and links nominal dynamics to a micro-founded money-demand function. Analytical results and a causal diagram clarify how energy shocks propagate through fiscal spending, output, money demand, and the price level. The framework avoids stock-flow inconsistencies common in informal treatments of energy-backed issuance.

title: How Courts Analyze Duty and Foreseeability in Third-Party Crime Cases
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Courts Analyze Duty and Foreseeability in Third-Party Crime Cases
detail.abstract:
When crime occurs in connection with a public event, lawsuits are almost inevitable. Claims may stem from violence during the event, during crowd control or dispersal, or after the event has ended as attendees move into surrounding public areas. Plaintiffs often contend that organizers, businesses, or municipalities should have foreseen the danger and acted to prevent it. Washington courts, however, do not approach these cases through the lens of sympathy or hindsight, and they have consistently declined to broaden private liability based on generalized fears of crime.

This article explores how Washington courts decide whether an event organizer or business owes a legal duty for the criminal acts of unknown third parties. Examining incidents that occur during events, during crowd management and dispersal, and after events conclude, it shows why negligence claims frequently fail at the duty stage. Under Washington law, foreseeability is a threshold legal determination reserved for the court. It requires specific, concrete facts, including evidence of prior similar incidents, rather than abstract assessments of risk.

Drawing on decisions from the Washington Supreme Court and the Court of Appeals, the article explains why businesses are not insurers of public safety and why security planning does not create unlimited responsibility. It also highlights why timing, location, and control are central to the analysis, particularly as an event winds down and responsibility shifts to public streets and law enforcement. By defining these limits, the article offers practical guidance for event organizers, businesses, municipalities, and litigators confronting third party crime claims tied to public events.

The percentage of residents with a positive WTP changed from 29.7% before the event to 39.3% immediately after the event, while average WTP increased significantly from €3.58 to €4.45, leading to an increase of residents’ valuation from €5.8 million to €7.1 million. Additionally, following the event in the media and attending the event play an important role in explaining residents’ WTP.

title: PKK’s ‘Peoples’ Brotherhood’ Has No Place in the Middle East

detail.title: PKK’s ‘Peoples’ Brotherhood’ Has No Place in the Middle East
detail.abstract: The collapse of Kurdish security and de facto autonomy in Syria exposes the failure of the PKK’s “Peoples’ Brotherhood” doctrine. Repeated betrayals, forced displacement, and the absence of reciprocity from Turkish, Arab, and Iranian actors show that regional nationalism consistently overrides appeals to coexistence. Unilateral Kurdish concessions, including disarmament and political compromise, have produced no recognition of Kurdish rights. As the SDF faces retreat and Kurdish self-rule comes under existential threat, realism and reciprocity—not idealism—must guide Kurdish politics.

title: How Complex Are Financial Decisions? Evidence from Credit Card Choice

detail.title: How Complex Are Financial Decisions? Evidence from Credit Card Choice
detail.abstract: Complexity is increasingly recognized as a barrier to sound financial decisionmaking, yet no theoretical framework currently characterizes it. We propose a framework that quantifies the complexity of financial decisions based on their computational demands and apply it to binary credit card choices. Using a combined behavioral and eye-tracking experiment, we show that complexity, rather than inattention or limited financial literacy, drives mistakes, and that it disproportionately burdens cardholders who carry a balance, for whom the stakes are highest. Our findings suggest that complexity is a fundamental barrier to optimal financial decision-making, even in seemingly simple choices.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how regulatory technology (RegTech) programmes operate as architectures of social ordering, drawing on Luhmann's social systems theory. We investigate how programmes simultaneously bridge functional systems, create inclusion/exclusion dynamics, generate complexity, and require legitimation through secondorder observation mechanisms. Design/Methodology/Approach: Using a dataset of RegTech startup deals from a leading venture capital database, we employ propensity score matching (PSM), mediation analysis, and interaction models to test five hypotheses that connect Luhmannian concepts to empirical outcomes. Findings: We identify three fundamental paradoxes: (1) High interface capacity, the ability to translate between regulatory and economic systems, increases funding by 47.1% (PSM); (2) Programmatic translation between functional system logics shows synergistic effects (β = 0.173, p < 0.05); (3) 21.3% of VC legitimacy effects operate through secondorder observation mechanisms; (4) Global positioning amplifies (rather than mitigates) Western advantages (β = 0.565, p < 0.05); and (5) Technology intensity paradoxically generates organizational complexity despite simplification goals (β = 0.165, p < 0.001). Originality: This is the first empirical study to operationalize Luhmann's programme concept in startup analysis, demonstrating how programmes function as decision premises that bridge functional systems while reproducing global stratification.

title: Should Partially Cooperating Firms Care for Consumers?
affiliations: Institute for Economic Sciences

detail.title: Should Partially Cooperating Firms Care for Consumers?
detail.abstract: This paper considers a multi-stage game model with two partially cooperating firms whose objective functions include maximizing not only their own profits but also a portion of their rivals' profits. In the first stage, each firm independently and simultaneously decides whether to incorporate consumer surplus into its objective function. In the second stage, any firm that chooses to do so selects its level of consumer orientation. In the third stage, after observing the rival's choices in the first and second stages, each firm independently and simultaneously chooses its output level. The paper characterizes the equilibrium of this model.

title: Gender Bias in Performance Evaluation: Experimental Evidence from Repeated Retention Decisions
affiliations: Management Development Institute Gurgaon

detail.title: Gender Bias in Performance Evaluation: Experimental Evidence from Repeated Retention Decisions
detail.abstract: Gender bias in performance evaluation can misallocate talent and reduce firm productivity, particularly in developing countries where formal HR systems are weak and individual contributions are difficult to observe. This study provides causal evidence on how performance transparency and the costliness of biased decisions influence gender bias in leader decision-making over multiple rounds. In an incentivized experiment, male leaders evaluated two-member teams in a male-typed prediction task, inferring individual contributions based on randomly assigned perceived gender, with treatments exogenously varying whether individual performance is ambiguous or partially observable, and whether replacement decisions incur financial costs. Under performance ambiguity, female-perceived team members are 33-40.5% more likely to be replaced, with bias concentrated in mid-performing teams where subjective inference is most salient. Making individual performance observable reduces, but does not eliminate, this gap, as female-perceived members must outperform male-perceived counterparts by 16.8-21% to achieve equal retention, consistent with attribution bias. Imposing financial costs on replacements further reduces discrimination. These results show that gender bias persists across repeated evaluations and manifests as systematic performance penalties for female-perceived team members, distorting retention decisions but can be partially mitigated through low-cost informational and incentive-based interventions.

title: Why Companies turn Too Late: Strategic Inertia from Startup to Scale-up
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Why Companies turn Too Late: Strategic Inertia from Startup to Scale-up
detail.abstract: Strategic failure is often explained ex post by poor leadership, insufficient foresight, or adverse external shocks. This paper advances an alternative perspective: strategic inertia is a stage-dependent structural outcome rather than a managerial pathology, emerging naturally as firms transition from exploration to scale. We model corporate decision-making as an evolutionary process shaped by three interacting forces: external pressure transmission, internal information integrity, and temporal irreversibility of strategic commitments. As firms grow, operational routines, performance metrics, and governance layers crystallize into stable structures that improve efficiency but simultaneously attenuate the transmission of external signals and delay corrective action. This trade-off produces a predictable dynamic: firms increasingly require stronger evidence to justify strategic change precisely when the cost of delay is rising most rapidly. The paper distinguishes three governance regimes across the firm lifecycle-exploration (startup), stabilization (scale-up), and inflection (strategic survival)-and shows how decision thresholds, error correction speed, and irreversibility evolve across these regimes. We demonstrate that "turning too late" is not an anomaly restricted to large incumbents, but a systematic risk that emerges as soon as organizations begin to scale, formalize metrics, and lock in operating assumptions. To operationalize this framework, we propose a small set of diagnostic indicators for governance and strategy teams, including measures of pressure transmission, signal integrity, and decision lockin. Through analytical reasoning and illustrative dynamic models, we show how these indicators can serve as early warning signals of strategic delay, well before performance deterioration becomes visible. The findings suggest that effective corporate governance is not primarily about improving foresight or incentives, but about maintaining structural conditions that preserve responsiveness under growth. The paper concludes with implications for board design, strategic tempo governance, and organizational interventions aimed at preventing delayed strategic turns across all stages of firm development.

title: Do Maximum Point Scales Influence Student Performance? Evidence from a Field Experiment
affiliations: Management Development Institute Gurgaon, Saint Mary's College of Maryland and Inclusion Economics India Center

detail.title: Do Maximum Point Scales Influence Student Performance? Evidence from a Field Experiment
detail.abstract: Educational assessments inform critical public policy decisions affecting student progression, institutional accountability, and resource allocation. Yet many assessment design features, including the maximum point scale used to score exams, are guided by administrative convention rather than empirical evidence. This study examines whether altering exam point scales affects student effort or performance when grading standards and underlying incentives remain unchanged. We report evidence from a preregistered field experiment involving 1,235 undergraduate students at a large university in India, where identical multiple-choice exams were framed as either 20-point or 100-point assessments and administered under natural testing conditions. Across measures of test performance and multiple proxies for test-taking effort, we find no statistically or economically meaningful effects of point-scale variation. These null effects are consistent across low and high-stakes exams, different test segments, and student subgroups defined by gender and prior ability. For policymakers, the results indicate important limits to numerical framing as a behavioral tool in assessment design and suggest that commonly adjusted, low-cost administrative features may not reliably influence student behavior. More broadly, the findings underscore the need for rigorous empirical evaluation of behavioral design interventions before their adoption in education policy.

detail.title: MSME Technology Development Centres' Influence: A Novel Perspective on the Indian Knowledge System
detail.abstract: The backbone of India's economy comprises a large number of micro, small and mediumsized enterprises; which contributes for employment of more than 110 million citizens, over 30% to the country's GDP, and almost 45% of its exports. Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, has been established Technology Centre Systems Programme to improve technology, innovation, and reduce the technological gap for small to medium-sized enterprises. The programme establishes Technology Centres, which are also known as Technology Development Centres. This paper studies how Traditional Discipline Centres, or TDCs, may be used as a mechanism for the fusion of Indian knowledge systems with contemporary technology and innovation. This analysis suggests that there are improvements in economic resilience and in the skills required for green entrepreneurship. This is based on the information available in government and academic papers and case studies. In 2024, over 330,000 trainees have been equipped with skills via these training centres, and more than 33,000 companies have received support, which helped these companies to experience productivity gains of as much as 35%. Businesses that use the IKS model are KVIC and Khadi. Together, they managed to generate sales of over 115,000 crore rupees. Notwithstanding the advancements made, there are still a number of issues with IKS integration which prevent innovation that has become deeply ingrained in the company's culture from flourishing. The proposed policy framework includes strategies to achieve equitable economic development and recommends the use of a technology and innovation strategy to fix these gaps. This strategy is in line with the Centre's 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' mission, and is also aimed at enhancing the competitiveness of the MSMEs. There is a report which underscores the requirement of policy improvements to achieve more synergy between TDC and IKS and points out where research is lacking in the field of scalable technology frameworks.

title: Leveraging Dynamic Mixture of Experts in Pinn for Bernoulli Free Boundary
affiliations: Yerevan State University, Sharif University of Technology, Sharif University of Technology and Royal Institute of Technology (KTH)

detail.title: Leveraging Dynamic Mixture of Experts in Pinn for Bernoulli Free Boundary
detail.abstract: In this work, we experiment with applying the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture within the context of the Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) framework to solve Bernoulli-type free boundary problems and propose a novel architecture-Dynamic Mixture-of-Experts Physics-Informed Neural Networks (DMoE-PINNs)-for more adaptability. While classical PINNs face limitations in handling complex, heterogeneous domains, the Mixture-of-experts paradigm enhances performance by allocating subnetworks (experts) to distinct spatial regions via a gating mechanism. We extend this idea by introducing an output-aware gating strategy, where the gating network utilizes not only spatial inputs but also an intermediate prediction of the solution. This context-enriched gating enables dynamic and adaptive expert assignment based on both geometric and functional information, improving specialization and reducing redundancy. DMoE-PINN for Bernoulli Free Boundary Our experiments on scalar and system variants of Bernoulli free boundary problems demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy, convergence stability, and computational efficiency over both classical PINNs and standard MoE-PINNs. We further show the effectiveness of DMoE-PINNs in non-convex and irregular domains, where classical methods often struggle. The framework supports sparsity regularization and model pruning, offering a scalable and interpretable solution for complex partial differential equations.

title: Impact of Flood on Bangladesh's Economy: A Case on Floods in Sylhet

detail.title: Impact of Flood on Bangladesh's Economy: A Case on Floods in Sylhet
detail.abstract: Bangladesh is historically known as a disaster-prone country; recent flooding has impacted the districts of Sylhet and Sunamganj in Bangladesh. The study attempts to analyze the economic impacts of flooding. The analysis revealed that the devastating flooding in Sylhet and Sunamganj had caused a significant economic disaster. It found that the damage of crops, the death of livestock, and the deterioration of the poultry and fisheries leading drivers of economic losses. The analysis estimates that the economic losses will approach 6,000 billion BDT. In Bangladesh, unplanned infrastructure development and road construction are the major human-induced causes of a massive flood. To minimize flood induced calamities and economic losses, the government should make environment-friendly development policies.

detail.abstract: Our research analyzes the role of an immediate needs annuity (INA) as a late-life insurance product. The market for traditional long-term care insurance (LTCI) is quite small in high-income countries, even those that lack universal insurance. For example, in the United States, only about 10% of individuals aged 61 or over held policies between 1992 and 2012, even though care costs can be extremely burdensome for individuals to bear.1 Moreover, some individuals are denied coverage at any price (Hendren, 2013; Braun et al., 2019), and some policyholders lapse their policies and forego all benefits (Friedberg et al., 2023). Theoretical calculations show that over a large part of the wealth distribution much of the gain from holding LTCI in the United States accrues not to policyholders but to the government in the form of lower Medicaid outlays (Brown & Finkelstein, 2008). In short, LTCI policies don't significantly reduce financial risk and might even increase it, while low take-up leaves the government bearing high costs. In their absence, income annuities (annuities that pay an income stream for life) might fill a similar insurance function for individuals facing high care costs late in life, and thus the risk of spending all their wealth before they die. However, in the United States, income annuities aren't medically underwritten, which makes them a poor deal for individuals needing care, nor are they sold to individuals at very advanced ages. This leaves a missing market for individuals seeking to insure consumption or bequests late in life.

detail.title: Barriers to Science Communication
detail.abstract: The contemporary collapse of democratic discourse is frequently attributed to failures of individual morality or education. Such positions harden the polarized voter to dig in and more strongly resist obvious cause. This paper proposes an alternative framework: that the polarization of the electorate is a predictable thermodynamic outcome of a specific topological architecture. By mapping the political landscape onto topologically isomorphic principles of electromagnetism, we identify the Political Egoist as the external Field Intensity (H), the Algorithmic Media Machine as the engine of circulation, and the Electorate as distinct agents subject to alignment. Applying Green's Theorem, we demonstrate how a voter's continuous traversal of digital media cycles is isomorphic to a closed-loop path integral. In a healthy information environment, this cycle would be conservative, allowing the voter to return to their initial state with no net loss of perspective. However, the algorithmic amplification of hyper-partisan rhetoric ensures this field is non-conservative. Consequently, the cognitive work performed to traverse a complete narrative cycle is non-zero. The voter is compelled to expend non-trivial cognitive energy to defend their doctrinal position against the deluge of conflicting data.

detail.abstract: Amid rising global concerns over environmental degradation and resource depletion, the pursuit of sustainable waste management practices has become a pressing priority for governments, industries, and communities. However, traditional waste management systems often suffer from persistent inefficiencies including limited transparency, weak traceability, and siloed data management that hinder the transition to a truly circular and sustainable economy. This study investigates the transformative potential of blockchain technology to address these challenges and drive sustainable innovation in waste management. By conducting a structured literature review, the paper identifies critical gaps in current systems and explores how blockchain-based solutions such as smart contracts, real-time waste traceability, and incentive-driven recycling schemes can promote greater accountability, stakeholder collaboration, and the adoption of sustainable practices. The study further highlights practical applications, examines implementation challenges, and outlines future research directions to support the integration of blockchain technology in building resilient, transparent, and circular waste management ecosystems.

detail.abstract: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) are widely regarded as the gold standard for causal inference across medicine, economics, psychology, and public policy. Their inferential authority rests on an implicit behavioral assumption rarely stated explicitly: that participants behave as sentiment-neutral, mechanically compliant units whose retention is independent of trust, fairness, dignity, or institutional legitimacy. In practice, human subjects are not epistemic particles; they are moral agents embedded in social and emotional ecologies. Evidence from psychology, behavioral economics, law, and development economics shows that heterogeneity in moral sentiments systematically shapes participation, retention, and compliance, thereby violating the assumptions required for unbiased estimation. This paper introduces the Emotionally and Ethically Informed Randomized Controlled Trial (EEI-RCT), a conceptual and formal framework that embeds fairness and institutional legitimacy directly into the experimental data-generating process. We formalize an Equitable Inference Framework (EIF) that generalizes classical RCT objectives by accounting for subgroup-level inferential inequities arising from fairness-sensitive attrition. A semi-formal result demonstrates that the standard Average Treatment Effect (ATE) estimator becomes biased whenever retention depends on perceived fairness or institutional trust, even under perfect randomization. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we illustrate how structured moral heterogeneity distorts treatment-effect estimates in two health-economics settings: a hypertension drug trial and a vaccine-incentive program. By integrating moral ecology (Smith), institutional legitimacy (Calabresi), and heterogeneous participation in development economics (Kremer and Duflo), this paper advances a new paradigm: causal inference is reliable only when experimental institutions are morally legitimate for all subgroups. Simulation-based pretesting thus emerges as a fifth evidentiary category in causal methodology, complementing observational, experimental, qualitative, and theoretical approaches.

detail.abstract: The ascendant trend in relation to the use of facial recognition technologies (FRTs) for surveillance purposes across a heterogeneity of regime types and geographical regions has raised concerns pertaining to the erosion of the right to privacy and, in turn, the stymieing of political participation in public spaces. This chapter undertakes an analysis of the right to privacy in the context of FRTs in the Global South. To that end, it will chart the legal framework pertaining to privacy in the Global South, the ramifications of the rampant use of FRTs for privacy and also—importantly—for democratic participation. The authors argue that the centrality of the informational conception of privacy in the existing legal framework provides insufficient safeguards against rising digital authoritarianism. This chapter will, instead, argue in favour of the entrenchment of a broader, overarching right to privacy that accounts for both its decisional and informational aspects, which insulates political participation from the debilitating effects of state surveillance in the Global South.

detail.abstract: This working paper shall focus on sensitivity analysis, modelling, and forecasting of market demand to cope with uncertainty in the decision-making process. In addition, this paper also aims to provide the reader with an intuitive and practical experience of the optimisation tools of microeconomics, coupled with time series econometrics methods applied with R software. The strong interest in data from the public transit sector in this empirical research is linked to the fact that it is undoubtedly one of the sectors likely to play an important role in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in future smart cities, which is all the more interesting as Toronto is Canada's largest municipality in terms of population. Indeed, public transit is a service that is beneficial to society for all its positive externalities. These benefits include accessibility and social equity in terms of fares and reduced road congestion, and, by extension, the fight against atmospheric pollution by reducing riders' CO2 emissions through public transport. Findings. (i) We shall provide a price-demand sensitivity model (fare in C$) for ridership demand inside the Toronto city area from 1969 to 2019 as well as the derivation of short-and long-term elasticities. We shall also provide, through modelling and forecasting, insight into future demand trends considering pre-and postpandemic scenarios. It is clear that one of the most remarkable points to emerge from the transit data in recent times is that the effects of the pandemic crisis have slowed ridership demand by almost half (225 million riders in 2020) compared to the previous trend (525.5 million riders in 2019) in the City of Toronto (TTC operating service area only), causing a structural break in the time series data, also observed in the TTC's latest report (only 197.8 million riders in 2021). This is not an isolated case for the city of Toronto, as Montreal (only 200 million users in 2020 compared to 426 million in 2019) and most of the major metropolitan cities in the world that were affected also experienced the same slowdown in demand due to reduced activity during the pandemic. (ii) Using our estimated market demand model for transit in the city of Toronto, we will attempt to estimate the optimal price and the price at which consumers are no longer willing to pay. And since this study concerns a public transit company in the form of a natural monopoly commonly referred to as a state monopoly, we shall draw on the seminal work and contributions of Frank Ramsey and Marcel Boiteux (Ramsey-Boiteux pricing rule) to understand the optimal pricing behaviour of this type of network infrastructure. The aim of this research will therefore also be to understand, beyond the elements of microeconomic optimization, that the nature of the company is at the center of its interests, which has a considerable influence on certain aspects that determine its business model and in particular its pricing behaviour (Baumol, 1959).

title: Forecast Value Under Adaptive Decision Rules
affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Students, Norwegian University of Science and Technology  and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

detail.title: Forecast Value Under Adaptive Decision Rules
detail.abstract: Decision-making in finance, energy, and operations is increasingly data-driven, where forecasts provide essential inputs for planning, trading, and operational control. They typically inform decisions through forecast-dependent policies that prescribe how actions should be taken based on the available predictions. However, organizations usually have access to a limited set of forecasting models and cannot obtain a forecast that is perfectly tailored to every decision. This complicates evaluation, as the economic value of a forecast inherently depends on how it is used in decision-making. Traditional forecast evaluation approaches typically ignore this decision context. Instead, they focus primarily on predictive accuracy and compare forecast performance under a single, fixed decision policy, making it difficult to determine whether the observed performance differences reflect forecast quality or the decision policy. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive forecast evaluation framework that assumes decision-makers can adjust their policies in response to forecast performance. We model the decision-maker as a learning agent that selects the policy parameters best suited to each forecast, capturing how AI-enabled decision-support systems adapt their behavior to data. We demonstrate how this adaptation improves economic evaluation and helps isolate the true forecast value using a trading application with day-ahead electricity price forecasts in the German market. We evaluate a rich set of forecasting models alongside decision rules, ranging from simple heuristics to adaptive machine-learning-based policies. Our results show that adaptive decision-aware evaluation policies reduce performance gaps between forecasts and offer a more accurate representation of forecast value in AI-driven decision settings.

title: What drives the spatiotemporal evolution of land use conflicts? Evidence of threshold effects from 19 Chinese urban agglomerations
affiliations: Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment Chinese Academy of Sciences, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: What drives the spatiotemporal evolution of land use conflicts? Evidence of threshold effects from 19 Chinese urban agglomerations
detail.abstract: Land use conflicts (LUCs) have emerged as a critical constraint on regional sustainable development. However, existing research predominantly focuses on single-dimensional conflict identification, lacking systematic comparative analysis and composite assessment at the urban agglomeration scale. This study employs multi-source data from 19 Chinese urban agglomerations spanning 2000–2020 to construct a land use assessment framework that integrates structural and functional conflicts. Utilizing spatial Durbin models, machine learning, and generalized additive models, it systematically reveals the spatiotemporal evolution patterns and driving mechanisms of LUCs. The findings indicate: (1) LUCs exhibited a phased pattern of 'initial rise followed by decline,' with significant intensification occurring between 2000 and 2010, gradually easing post-2010 alongside ecological civilization strategies; (2) Spatial patterns demonstrate an 'east-high, west-low' divergence, with core eastern agglomerations such as Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and the Yangtze River Delta Urban Agglomeration enduring persistent high conflict pressures, while northwestern regions experience lower conflict intensity; (3) The intensity of human footprint index (HFI) and terrain roughness index are dominant factors. Conflicts in eastern urban clusters primarily arise from high-intensity development pressures, whereas northwestern regions are constrained by topographical features. Key factors exhibit pronounced threshold effects: conflicts intensify sharply when HFI intensity and road network density exceed critical values. Vegetation cover demonstrates a non-monotonic influence, with the most acute contradictions between ecological conservation and development demands occurring in areas of moderate cover. This research provides scientific support for optimizing national spatial patterns, promoting coordinated regional development, and achieving dual carbon goals.

title: Organizing Collective Action for Sufficiency in Community-Based Organizations: Cross-Cultural Patterns
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Organizing Collective Action for Sufficiency in Community-Based Organizations: Cross-Cultural Patterns
detail.abstract: Sufficiency is the culture and practice of “enoughness,” increasingly relevant in times of deepening social stratification and ecological degradation. Studying nineteen community-based organizations (CBOs) across land and food systems, energy and finance, housing and mobility, healthcare and education, intentional communities and governance systems, this paper asks: how do CBOs organize collective action so that it prioritizes meeting needs rather than generating ungeneralizable excess? Using a qualitative multiple-case design, it draws on semi-structured interviews with key representatives from each CBO and secondary sources, and analyzes them through abductive thematic coding. The results show that the featured CBOs face various social and ecological stressors, and in response they (1) organize collective action through the primacy of other-regarding intent centred on access to needs satisfiers, livelihood stability, and ecological stewardship; (2) cultivate autonomy, participation, and local control; (3) pool, share, and mutualize resources to provide safety nets and distribute risks; (4) develop community-based monitoring, co-created rules, and transparency that foster trust; and (5) invest in knowledge sharing and appropriate technologies that enhance capabilities. Together, these elements function as sufficiency-supporting microinstitutions—an “immune system” steering collective action to prioritize needs. Non-oligarchic, trust-based, autonomy-supportive arrangements of the studied CBOs offer instructions for organizing provisioning systems that secure basic needs within planetary boundaries.

title: When the Warrior Trembles: Mental Health Lessons from Arjuna & Krishna

detail.title: When the Warrior Trembles: Mental Health Lessons from Arjuna & Krishna
detail.abstract: Mental health is now recognized as central to human wellbeing across disciplines, yet the role of classical spiritual texts in addressing psychological distress remains underexplored. This paper examines the Bhagavad Gita as an early, profound framework for understanding mental health through the dialogue between the trembling warrior Arjuna and Sri Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Arjuna’s paralysis, despair, and moral conflict closely parallel modern concepts of anxiety, depression, and moral injury—defined as psychological harm arising from actions that violate deeply held ethical values. Drawing upon interdisciplinary insights, including prior collaborative research with neurologists and psychiatrists published in the Journal of Religion and Health, this work situates the Gita as a holistic therapeutic text. It highlights how Krishna’s guidance integrates emotional validation, ethical clarity, and transformative action. The paper argues that healing emerges through sincerity, right action without attachment, and surrender, offering the Gita as a timeless reservoir of psychological resilience and moral restoration for contemporary life.

detail.abstract: Ditfurth and Arzt highlight the continuous, evolutionary process of general vehicle development from the horse-drawn carriage to the steam vehicle and eventually up to the internal combustion engine vehicle of today. Mutation and selection shaped this development to best meet customer needs. Technical, infrastructural and sociocultural requirements and needs are decisive. Thus, it was also a process of balancing different desires for human transportation and mobility culture: the vehicle as an urban, touring, racing, and luxury means of transport. Especially the transfer from the electric vehicle to the gasoline vehicle transformed the latter from a purely adventurous and speedy option to a more utilitarian mobility solution. Through the rising similarities in car features, price and the affordabilitysocioeconomic advantages of the gasoline car-became decisive prerequisites for the mass motorisation. In the 21st century the development of sustainable mobility solutions takes place between different drive systems. The acceptance of the public and the (potential) customers, as well as a sustainably value-creating business model for the OEMs and the customers, are prerequisites for the successful future of sustainable automotive mobility worldwide.

detail.abstract: In an era where AI-generated video and audio can convincingly imitate corporate leaders, the latency between misinformation and credible verification, Trust Velocity Gap (TVG) has collapsed to near zero. This paper argues that traditional crisis-response windows (e.g., 24 hours) are obsolete. Instead, a Zero-Hour mandate governs the trajectory of corporate reputational risk and stakeholder financial stability. We define the TVG, articulate a Zero Hour readiness framework, and propose metrics and governance mechanisms to protect long term value. Through theoretical framing and scenario analysis, the paper demonstrates that rapid, validated, pre-vetted communications within the first sixty minutes are determinative for investor confidence, employee trust, customer loyalty, and procurement stability.

detail.abstract: Digital twin technology originally developed in aerospace and manufacturing has rapidly emerged as a transformative paradigm in medicine. A medical digital twin is a dynamic, virtual representation of an individual patient that integrates biological, physiological, genetic, and environmental data to simulate health states and predict treatment outcomes. By enabling real-time monitoring, predictive modeling, and personalized intervention strategies, digital twins promise to revolutionize clinical decision-making and precision medicine. This paper explores the conceptual foundations of digital twins in medicine, their technological architecture, current clinical applications, and the ethical, regulatory, and technical challenges that must be addressed for large-scale adoption. The study concludes that digital twins represent a critical bridge between computational biology and personalized healthcare, with the potential to significantly improve patient outcomes, reduce healthcare costs, and shift medicine from reactive to predictive care.

detail.abstract: This note examines how digital platforms in the sharing economy use information disclosure to shape user behavior, coordinate supply and demand, and manage operational performance. Drawing on examples from ride‑hailing, food delivery, freelance labor, and peer‑to‑peer markets, it synthesizes what platforms currently reveal in practice (such as wait‑time estimates, ratings, heatmaps, and demand forecasts) and connects these mechanisms to insights from operations management research. The discussion highlights key trade‑offs between transparency, control, efficiency, and trust, and outlines emerging challenges related to algorithmic personalization, cross‑market data sharing, and regulatory expectations. The note concludes by identifying promising directions for future Operations Management research on platform information disclosure.

detail.abstract:
Despite unprecedented advances in biomedical science ranging from gene editing and cell therapies to precision oncology and RNA-based medicines many breakthrough therapies fail to reach patients at scale. This paradox reflects a growing commercialization crisis in advanced biomedicine, where scientific success does not reliably translate into clinical or societal impact. This article examines the structural, economic, regulatory, and institutional barriers that prevent promising biomedical innovations from progressing beyond the laboratory or early clinical trials. Drawing on evidence from translational research, health economics, and innovation studies, the paper argues that the crisis is not primarily scientific but systemic. It concludes by proposing policy and market-oriented reforms to realign incentives, de-risk late-stage translation, and ensure that biomedical breakthroughs fulfill their therapeutic potential.

Keywords: biomedical commercialization, translational medicine, innovation failure, health economics, regulatory science, advanced therapies

detail.abstract:
There is currently little published literature because the Space Force is still in its preliminary stages, developing the elements that characterize an organization (Soto, 2023, p. 11). There are no quantitative performance studies; thus, the evidence is anecdotal. Currently, studies focus on technical integration rather than organizational or human integration. Many researchers believe that understanding the interdependent relationships among motivation, job performance, and job satisfaction is vital for addressing challenges and problems and is pertinent to organizations (Jalagat, 2016, pp. 36, 42).

This research applied the mediation models of Hayes (2022) to survey data from the 2024 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey.  Six-factor scores were derived from the 2024 FEVS questions. They are Public Service Motivation, Employee Engagement, Commitment, Resilience, Job Satisfaction, Job Performance, and Leadership.  Factor scores are derived from survey items that assess an employee’s experience with the organization and its leaders. They are combined into a single factor score for interpretation and/or analysis.

The PROCESS macro by Hayes (2022) in IBM SPSS Statistics version 30.0 estimates coefficients in mediation models and provides modern inferential methods for indirect effects, including bootstrap confidence intervals. In an intervening-variable model, variable X is posited to affect an outcome variable Y via one or more intervening variables, also called mediators.

Four mediation models were applied in this research: the relationship between resilience and job performance was mediated by job satisfaction and work engagement; whether work-life balance mediates the relationship between leadership and job satisfaction; if satisfaction and engagement were statistically significant mediators of the relationship between resilience and job performance, and whether public service motivation was a statistically significant mediator of the relationship between work engagement and job performance.

detail.title: Task Characteristics and Job Satisfaction: The Moderating Role of Automation
detail.abstract: Recent research on automation and job satisfaction points out that robotization negatively impacts workers’ well-being by inducing fear ofreplacement, questioning work meaningfulness and/or affecting workers’ mental health. Seeking to consider both risks as well as potential benefitsof automation, the present paper focuses on the role of task characteristics for job satisfaction, and it investigates the moderating role of automation.Specifically, we consider three important task characteristics that vary across occupations - routine-manuality, perception and manipulation,and social intelligence - and we study how the effects of these characteristics on workers’ well-being are moderated by automation. The empiricalanalysis makes use of a rich database for the Italian labor market. The econometric results point out that robotization positively moderates theeffects of task characteristics on job satisfaction. Workers in occupations that have higher automatability risks are precisely those that experiencemore benefits from the introduction of machines in the workplace. This result holds for workers with lower education levels, and those that havea permanent job contract.

detail.title: Report on Simplification of EU Financial Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 204
publicationDetails.journalName: European Banking Institute (EBI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This Report examines the systemic complexity of EU financial regulation and develops a structured and conceptually grounded framework for regulatory simplification. Covering banking, capital markets, insurance, and payments law, as well as selected cross-sectoral areas such as AML/CFT, digital finance, data governance, and sustainable finance, it argues that regulatory complexity in the EU has become cumulative and structural rather than incidental. Successive waves of legislation and supervision, driven by financial stability objectives, technological innovation, sustainability goals, and international standard-setting, have produced overlapping legal regimes, fragmented taxonomies, blurred institutional mandates, and an expanding reliance on highly technical and prescriptive rules.

The Report situates the simplification agenda within the broader EU policy context, including the Savings and Investments Union, recent institutional reports, and the European Commission’s simplification initiatives. It explicitly rejects any equation of simplification with deregulation, instead conceptualising simplification as a methodological and architectural exercise aimed at rationalising legal sources, stabilising definitions and taxonomies, and improving coherence across sectors and regulatory levels, with the objective of preserving substantive safeguards while enhancing clarity, accessibility, proportionality and effectiveness. Particular attention is devoted to institutional asymmetries across sectors, the erosion of the Lamfalussy framework, the hardening of soft law, and the interaction between EU and international regulatory standards.

On this basis, the Report advances a coherent set of policy proposals across institutional, substantive, and procedural dimensions. Institutionally, it calls for clearer mandates, legal status, and accountability of EU agencies, alongside a more balanced and coherent approach to supervisory centralisation beyond the banking sector. Substantively, it advocates restoring the hierarchy of regulatory sources envisaged by the Lamfalussy framework, refocusing Level-1 legislation on core principles, disciplining the use of Level-2 acts, and clarifying the legal effects of Level-3 soft law, combined with a systematic review and codification of definitions and taxonomies and a reduction of options and discretions where full harmonisation is feasible. Procedurally, it proposes a structured mapping of applicable rules across sectors and regulatory levels to identify overlaps and inconsistencies, complemented by coordinated reforms, regular evidence-based review cycles, and streamlined reporting through integrated systems and common data standards. It concludes that simplification is a prerequisite for the long-term effectiveness, legitimacy, and competitiveness of EU financial regulation, rather than an alternative to it.

title: The Dollar's Double Life: Not All Dollar Appreciations are Born Equal for the Cross-Currency Basis
affiliations: University of Essex - Department of Mathematics, Baum Tenpers Research Institute and Asian Institute of Management

detail.title: The Dollar's Double Life: Not All Dollar Appreciations are Born Equal for the Cross-Currency Basis

keywords: Dollar Appreciation Hedging Demand and Supply

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the relationship between the US dollar and cross-currency basis swap spreads. We show that the strength and direction of this relationship depend on the prevailing regime of the broad dollar. The evidence suggests that the well-documented "dollar appreciates, basis widens" result holds primarily when the dollar is in a low or intermediate regime. However, Once the dollar transitions into a high regime, this association either weakens or reverses: a stronger dollar no longer widens the basis, and may tighten it. Our findings reveal that not all dollar appreciations are created equal. For the same magnitude of dollar appreciation, basis spreads tend to widen significantly more in low-or intermediate-dollar regimes than in high-dollar regime. We explain these results through a theoretical framework grounded in hedging demand and supply imbalances and validate them empirically using the term structure of cross-currency basis swap spreads of G10 currencies.

title: The Economic Consequences of Regulatory Failure: Evidence from the 2017 KPMG-PCAOB Audit Inspection Scandal
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business, National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore (NUS) - Sustainable & Green Finance Institute (SGFIN) and National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

detail.title: The Economic Consequences of Regulatory Failure: Evidence from the 2017 KPMG-PCAOB Audit Inspection Scandal
detail.abstract: We study the 2017 KPMG-PCAOB audit inspection scandal, an extreme case of revolving door gone wrong with the potential to compromise the integrity of U.S. audit supervision, and examine how this detected regulatory failure affects client banks that are uninvolved in the misconduct but named in court transcripts. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that treatment banks significantly reduce mortgage credit supply following the scandal, originating about 969 fewer mortgages per bank-year on average, which corresponds to an approximate $138 million reduction in annual mortgage credit. These adjustments are concentrated among banks under greater ex ante scrutiny from banking regulators, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau. Treatment banks also improve mortgage service quality following the scandal. Ex post, these banks strengthen their capital buffers and experience fewer enforcement actions. Overall, our findings suggest that extreme regulatory failures can have real economic consequences beyond directly regulated entities, prompting client banks in our setting to reallocate resources away from expanding credit volume toward improving service quality under intensified regulatory oversight.

title: The Impact of Multi-acquiring in the Payment System: Evidence from Uruguayan Financial Inclusion Program

detail.title: The Impact of Multi-acquiring in the Payment System: Evidence from Uruguayan Financial Inclusion Program

publicationDetails.journalName: Inter-American Development Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the transition from exclusive card network-acquirer relationships to a multi-acquiring model. Using the case of Uruguay’s adoption of multi-acquiring in 2022, as part of a broader financial inclusion program. We document significant market dynamics, including restructured relationships among incumbents and new market entrants. Our analysis, leveraging the Herfindahl- Hirschman Index, reveals decreased market concentration across all payment segments. While fee reductions were initially driven by a government-sponsored price agreement, the increased competition fostered by multi-acquiring stabilized these rates even after the agreement was no longer in effect. Large merchants benefited from enhanced efficiency, but small merchants faced adaptation challenges. These findings underscore the complexities of regulating two-sided payment markets and emphasize the need for balanced interventions to ensure a competitive payment ecosystem.

title: Connectivity and Misallocation in Multi-unit Firms

detail.title: Connectivity and Misallocation in Multi-unit Firms

publicationDetails.journalName: Inter-American Development Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the causal effect of reducing distance-related frictions with headquarters on branch outcomes in multi-unit firms in B razil. Exploiting the introduction of new airline routes, we compare branches that gain a direct flight t o t heir headquarters with otherwise similar branches in the same location that do not. In contrast to prior findings from high-income country settings, improved connectivity with headquarters lowers 12-month survival and, conditional on survival, reduces service and production employment. To interpret these results, we develop a model with three distancedependent frictions: i) internal coordination costs of delivering headquarters inputs to branches; ii) client-service costs when serving markets without a local branch; and iii) a moral-hazard friction whereby distance amplifies l ocal m anagers’ incentives to over-hire. Consistent with the model’s predictions, survival declines are larger at closer branches, while employment reductions are concentrated at more distant branches and in firms with lower headquarters b andwidth. The model clarifies how the impact of reduced frictions with headquarters depends on pre-existing distortions and reconciles heterogeneous connectivity effects observed across developing- and high-income contexts.

title: Are All Prior Art References Becoming Analogous in the AI Age?
affiliations: Berkeley Centre for Law and Technology

detail.title: Are All Prior Art References Becoming Analogous in the AI Age?
detail.abstract:
This Article focuses on an important doctrinal question: Are all prior art references becoming “analogous” in the AI age? While this question may seem trivial at first glance, it is one of the key inquiries that would significantly shape the specific contour of patent law in an age with super-efficient machines.

As state-of-the-art (SOTA) artificial intelligence is integrated into research and development, a new inventing paradigm is taking shape: Centaur (Human + AI) Inventing Synergy. In this paradigm, a cognitive division of labor has formed between human researchers and AI. While AI possesses unprecedented “horsepower” for solving problems, it remains inherently limited in creative problem defining—the stronghold of human faculty for finding and framing original problems in complex, real-world contexts.

This paradigm shift poses systemic challenges to patent law. Building on previous work regarding the rise of Centaur Inventors, this Article focuses on the US Patent Act Section 103 non-obviousness doctrine. Under the Graham-KSR framework, whether a claimed invention is adequately creative is a legal question based on the scope and content of prior art and the skill level of a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA). Unlike the Section 102 novelty doctrine, U.S. patent law imposes a filter for Section 103: for a prior art reference to be considered, it must first be found "analogous" to the claimed invention.

Under Federal Circuit precedent, a reference is analogous if it is from the same field of endeavor or is "reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the inventor is involved." This requirement recognizes that a PHOSITA cannot be aware of every field and serves as a vital safeguard against potential hindsight bias. Following the Supreme Court's decision in KSR v. Teleflex, the analogous art inquiry has become the primary doctrinal firewall against an overbroad determination of obviousness. 

Despite its post-KSR strategic primacy, the methodology remains vague. A careful reading of Federal Circuit case law reveals a persistent doctrinal void: the Court frequently defaults to the inventor’s own subjective, ex post problem statement—often drawn from the patent specification—rather than independently reconstructing how a PHOSITA would have framed the problem ex ante.

In the AI age, this "specification trap" risks rendering all prior art analogous. As illustrated by thought experiments involving the Wright brothers’ 3D dynamic control and origami-inspired surgical tools, once a human achieves the creative leap of framing a "catalytic problem," AI’s boundless connectivity can retrospectively bridge disparate fields, making the resulting solution appear inevitable. This Article illustrates how an unexamined analogous art doctrine systematically penalizes the most creative human leaps.

To preserve the incentive for human "architects" of invention, this Article proposes a rigorous adherence to the Federal Circuit’s teaching in Donner v. Pro Stage (2020). Notably, although the Donner decision was not originally intended to address AI-related challenges, its mandate provides a vital corrective for the current era. By requiring that the "problem to be solved" be identified from the objective, ex ante perspective of the PHOSITA, the Donner guardrail prevents the infinite interpolation of AI from collapsing distinct fields into a single pool of analogous art. Ultimately, patent law must evolve to properly value and protect the crucial human sparkle: the act of creative problem-defining.

title: Social Preferences for Public Provision of Services: Experimental Evidence from Latin America
affiliations: Centro de Investigación y Docencia Económicas (CIDE) - Center for Research and Teaching of Economics (CIDE), Students, Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and Inter-American Development Bank

detail.title: Social Preferences for Public Provision of Services: Experimental Evidence from Latin America

publicationDetails.journalName: Inter-American Development Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how individuals in six Latin American countries value public versus private provision of education and healthcare using a survey experiment. Respondents were randomly assigned to vignettes that vary income, service quality, and provider type. Perceived quality is the main driver of choices: the probability of selecting a private provider roughly doubles when public quality falls from 80 to 20 percent, while income has a smaller effect. Higher institutional trust lowers the likelihood of switching to private providers but does not affect willingness to pay once individuals choose private provision. The multi-country design supports external validity and reveals similar behavioral responses across contexts. The results show that improving service quality and rebuilding institutional trust can reduce reliance on private provision.

title: Component-wise Latent Class Choice Model
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Component-wise Latent Class Choice Model
detail.abstract:
Understanding individual preference heterogeneity is a central challenge in discrete choice modeling. While the Latent Class Choice Model (LCCM) offers interpretable segmentation by grouping individuals with similar tastes, it imposes a restrictive structure in which all utility coefficients vary jointly within a single latent class. When heterogeneity arises independently across multiple attribute dimensions, this structure requires a combinatorial number of classes, leading to parameter redundancy, information dispersion, and statistical inefficiency.


To address these limitations, we propose the Component-wise Latent Class Choice Model (CLCCM). The CLCCM decomposes the utility function into analyst-defined components, each governed by its own latent class structure. Rather than assigning individuals to a single monolithic class, the model allows distinct class memberships for each utility component, with overall preference profiles formed as the Cartesian product of component-specific memberships. This structure parsimoniously captures multidimensional heterogeneity while preserving interpretability. We further develop a generalized EM algorithm with component-wise updates that guarantees monotonic likelihood improvement and stable estimation.


Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the CLCCM achieves superior statistical efficiency, more accurate recovery of utility coefficients and memberships, and more stable convergence than conventional LCCM specifications spanning the same heterogeneity space. An empirical application to discrete choice experiment data on breast cancer screening shows that the CLCCM uncovers interpretable behavioral segments associated with specific parts of the utility function that are conflated in standard models. Overall, the CLCCM provides a flexible and scalable framework that balances interpretability and efficiency for modeling multidimensional preference heterogeneity in applied choice analysis.

title: Strategic Interactions and Gender Cues: Evidence from Social Preference Games
